title: Maximum XOR With an Element From Array
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning per query versus offline queries sorted by limit with an incrementally built trie.

sections.title: Maximum XOR With an Element From Array

content.title: Maximum XOR With an Element From Array

blocks.text: Given an array nums and a list of queries, where each query is a pair (xi, mi), find for each query the maximum XOR of xi with any element of nums that is less than or equal to mi. If no element of nums is less than or equal to mi, the answer for that query is -1.

blocks.caption: Sort queries by their limit and grow one shared trie, instead of rescanning nums per query

blocks.title: Analogy: Best Match Within a Budget, Across Many Shopping Trips
blocks.text: Like making many separate shopping trips, each with its own spending limit, and each time searching among only the items priced within that trip's limit for the one item that best complements a given target combination.

blocks.caption: For each query, find the best XOR partner among only the elements at or below that query's limit

blocks.content: {"headers":["Query (xi, mi)","Allowed elements (at most mi)","Best XOR","Why"],"rows":[["(3, 1)","0, 1","3 XOR 0 = 3 is the best among these","3 XOR 0 = 3 beats 3 XOR 1 = 2, since 0 disagrees with 3 in more bit positions than 1 does"],["(1, 3)","0, 1, 2, 3","1 XOR 2 = 3 is the best among these","1 (binary 01) and 2 (binary 10) disagree in both bits, producing the largest possible 2-bit XOR"],["(5, 6)","0, 1, 2, 3, 4","5 XOR 2 = 7 is the best among these","5 (binary 101) and 2 (binary 010) disagree in every bit position, producing the maximum possible XOR for these values"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: a query whose limit is smaller than every element in nums
If no element of nums is small enough to qualify for a query's limit, that query's answer is -1, since no valid partner exists.

Before optimizing anything, notice the real inefficiency is not in any single query, it is in treating every query as if it were the very first one ever asked, rescanning and refiltering the same array from scratch every time.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Each individual query, "best XOR partner among elements at most m", is exactly the same greedy bit-trie problem as Maximum XOR of Two Numbers, just restricted to a filtered subset of nums.

Observation 2: Since every query is known in advance, this is an "offline" setting, not a live stream, so queries do not have to be answered in the order they were given; they can be reordered however is most convenient, as long as each answer is placed back at its original position.

Observation 3: If both nums and the queries are sorted by their limit value, then processing queries in increasing limit order means the set of "currently qualifying" elements only ever grows, one element added at a time, and never needs anything removed.

Observation 4: A single forward-moving pointer through sorted nums, combined with an incrementally growing trie that elements are inserted into and never removed from as each query's limit is reached, lets every query reuse all the trie-building work done for every earlier, smaller-limit query.

Whenever a batch of queries share a common filtering structure, like "elements at most m", consider processing them offline, sorted by that filter value, so a single incrementally growing data structure serves every query instead of being rebuilt from scratch each time.
This turns n times q independent element scans into one shared sweep, with the underlying per-query cost reduced to the same greedy trie walk already used for the pairwise maximum XOR problem.
For every query independently, scan through the entire array, filter out elements larger than the query's limit, and compute the XOR with every remaining element to find the best one.

items: For each query, scan the whole array.
Skip any element larger than the query's limit.
Compute the XOR of the query's value with every remaining element, tracking the best one.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: best starts at -1 for every query, directly matching the problem's required fallback answer when no element of nums ends up qualifying under that query's limit.
The if num <= m filter is checked before computing any XOR, so disqualified elements never influence the running best for that query.
Each query is handled with its own completely independent scan of nums, since the brute force intentionally does not try to share any work between queries.

blocks.text: Every query directly checks every qualifying element, so the true best XOR for each query is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(q times n), rescanning the whole array for every one of q queries.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the output.

Limitation: each query rescans the entire array from scratch, repeating the same filtering work and search for a similar limit across many queries, when processing all queries together in a smart order could reuse work between them.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force wastes effort in a specific, structural way: many queries share overlapping sets of qualifying elements, especially any two queries whose limits are close together, yet each one re-filters and re-scans the entire array as if starting from zero. The key unlock is realizing all queries are available upfront, so their processing order is a free choice, not fixed by the input order. Sorting queries by their limit value turns "which elements currently qualify" into a strictly growing set as processing proceeds: a query with a larger limit only ever needs the elements already inserted for smaller-limit queries, plus whatever newly qualifies in between. That means a single forward-only pointer through sorted nums, combined with a trie that only ever receives insertions and never deletions, correctly reflects the exact right candidate set at every query, without ever reprocessing an already-inserted element.

Sort both nums and the queries by their limit value. Process the queries in increasing order of their limit, and maintain a binary trie that gets incrementally built up: as each query is processed, insert every element of nums that is now small enough to qualify (using a pointer that only ever moves forward through the sorted nums array, never backward) before answering that query using a greedy trie walk. Since queries are handled in increasing limit order, every element that qualifies for an earlier query also automatically qualifies for every later one, so nothing ever needs to be removed from the trie.
Sort nums and queries by limit, incrementally inserting qualifying elements into a trie as queries are processed in increasing limit order.

blocks.caption: Optimized: sort queries by limit, incrementally build the trie, greedy walk per query

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((n plus q) times log(n plus q)) for sorting, plus O((n plus q) times 30) for the trie insertions and queries.
Space: O(n times 30), for the trie nodes.

Sorting queries by limit and only ever inserting elements forward through sorted nums guarantees that, at the moment any query is processed, the trie contains exactly the set of elements less than or equal to that query's limit, no more and no fewer, since every element with a smaller or equal value was already reached by the forward pointer, and no element with a larger value has been inserted yet. Because nothing is ever removed from the trie once inserted, every earlier query's insertion work is fully reused by every later query.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Condition","What it guarantees"],"rows":[["nums sorted ascending, queries sorted by limit ascending","The forward pointer only ever needs to move forward, never backward, to reach exactly the right qualifying prefix of nums for each query"],["Trie insertions only, never deletions","Every element inserted for an earlier, smaller-limit query remains available for every later, larger-limit query, with no repeated work"]]}

items: indexed_queries / order sorts query indices by their limit value, not the queries themselves, so each answer can still be placed back into results at its original position.
The while loop condition nums[num_index] <= m advances the shared pointer forward, inserting every newly-qualifying element into the trie exactly once, right before that query is answered.

Checking whether any element has qualified yet (num_index > 0) guards against answering a query with an empty trie, correctly leaving that query's result at its initialized -1 fallback instead of computing a meaningless XOR.
best_xor(x) is the exact same greedy opposite-bit trie walk used in Maximum XOR of Two Numbers, applied here against whatever subset of nums currently qualifies rather than the full array.

blocks.text: This is the classic "offline query" pattern: since all queries are known in advance, they can be reordered and processed together against an incrementally growing structure, turning what would otherwise be repeated per-query work into a single shared pass.

items: Forgetting to sort both nums and the queries by limit, which is what allows the single forward-moving pointer to correctly and completely track which elements qualify as processing proceeds.
Answering a query before any elements have qualified yet, instead of correctly returning -1 when the trie is still empty for that query's limit.
Writing each query's answer back using the sorted processing order's index instead of its original query index, which silently shuffles every answer to the wrong position in the output.

items: Emphasize explicitly why processing queries out of their original order is safe here: the final answers are placed back into a results array indexed by each query's original position, so reordering for processing efficiency never changes which answer belongs to which query.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Many queries, each filtered by some threshold, against the same underlying data" points toward offline processing: sort the queries by that threshold and build up a shared structure incrementally, instead of answering each query in isolation.

items: How would you handle queries arriving one at a time, live, where future queries cannot be seen in advance? The offline sort-by-limit trick no longer applies directly; a persistent or version-aware trie, or accepting a slower per-query rebuild, would be needed instead.

What if a query's condition were "at least m" instead of "at most m"? The sort direction and pointer direction would simply reverse, processing queries in decreasing limit order while a pointer moves backward through nums, inserting progressively smaller elements.

How would memory be reduced if nums were extremely large? Elements could be inserted into the trie and then discarded from any separate storage once inserted, since the trie itself is the only structure that needs to persist across queries.

Same "offline queries sorted by a threshold, processed against an incrementally growing structure" pattern as many range-query and Fenwick-tree or segment-tree offline problems outside of bit manipulation.
Same greedy opposite-bit trie walk as Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array, just applied to a filtered, incrementally growing subset instead of the full array at once.
Same "sort both sides and use a single forward pointer" technique as classic two-pointer merge-style problems, here applied to synchronize elements and queries by limit instead of by array position.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(q times n) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (offline queries sorted by limit, incremental trie): O((n plus q) log(n plus q)) time for sorting plus O((n plus q) times 30) for trie operations, O(n times 30) space.

items: Pattern: Offline queries sorted by limit, answered against an incrementally built binary trie
Core Idea: Reorder queries by their limit so the set of qualifying elements only ever grows, letting one shared trie and one forward pointer serve every query instead of rescanning per query
Time: O((n+q) log(n+q)) for sorting plus O((n+q) times 30) for trie operations
Space: O(n times 30), for the trie nodes

Most Important Observation: When all queries are known in advance and share a common filtering threshold, reordering them by that threshold turns repeated re-filtering into one shared incremental sweep
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Sort queries by limit, grow the trie, never shrink it
